BLADE BACK (CAMBERED SURFACE AREA)
A propeller blade has a curved or convex forward surface
called the blade back (a cambered face) that accelerates air
and reduces its pressure. This creates an INFLOW.

The blade also has a flat rear surface, known as the blade face

CHORD LINE
The chord line is an imaginary straight line stretching from the
centre of the leading edge to the centre of the trailing edge.

CHORD
The chord is the distance between the leading and training

HUB
All the propeller blades are secured to a hub and then the hub
is secured to the propeller drive shaft from the engine.

The Spinner is secured to the Hub by a back-plate. It is aerody-

PROPELLER OPERATION
• The propeller rotates.
• The blades force air rearwards.
• This creates a low-pressure area in front of the propel-
ler.
• The low-pressure area draws in more air (inflow).
• In this way the propeller creates a column of high-pres-
sure air moving from front to rear.
• The column of moving air produces thrust as a reaction.

VARIATIONS IN ANGLE OF ATTACK
If aircraft forward speed or engine RPM are changed, then the
direction of the relative airflow will also change. This will ‘ef-
fectively’ change the angle of attack.
CHANGES IN FORWARD SPEED
An increase in forward speed will change the direction of the
relative airflow and decrease the effective angle of attack. As
the angle of attack decreases; the load on the propeller is re-
duced.
Reduced propeller load allows the engine rpm to increase until
propeller load and engine rpm are balanced.
A decrease in forward speed will change the direction of the
relative airflow and increase the effective angle of attack. As
the angle of attack is increased the load on the propeller is in-
creased.
Increased propeller load reduces the engine rpm until the pro-
peller load and engine rpm are balanced.

SLIP STREAM EFFECT
If we take as an example the right-hand rotating engine again
another yawing effect is generated by the flowing air mass of
the propeller. It is named the slipstream effect. Air pushed back
by the propeller has two streams. One is axial stream, which
travel axially along the fuselage. The other stream - caused
mostly by the blade tips - flows around the surface of the air-
craft at an accelerated speed when compared to air flowing
over the surface outside the propeller disc.
On one side the control surfaces within the path of the slip-
stream benefit from the accelerated flow and become more
effective. The slipstream generated by the propeller also has
a whirling action as it flows aft. This rotating air mass on sin-
gle-engine aircraft, or aircraft with a propeller in the nose, ex-
perience a yawing action due to the striking of the air against
the vertical fin.
For right-hand rotating propellers, the aircraft tends to have
a yawing moment to the left. Slipstream effect is often com-
pensated by offsetting the vertical fin, incorporating a correc-
tive measure with the rudder, or applying a slight offset of the
thrust line of the engine by designing the engine mount with
a corrective installation angle. Such corrective measures may
also soften the effect of P-Factor. Fig 01. 25 - Slipstream effect

COMPOSITE PROPELLERS
As with other parts of the airplane, composite materials and
construction techniques have been adopted by the propeller
manufacturers. They offer numerous advantages, especially

are wound around a core. An attached erosion strip, when in-

SYSTEM
CONSTRUCTION
Planetary gear system consists of one or more gears (called
Planets) rotating around a central gear (Sun).
Another outer gear, a ring gear (Annulus) meshes with each of
the Planets during rotation. The planet gears are held together
in orbit around the Sun gear by a Carrier plate.
Fig 03. 40 - Planetary Gear System
This type of gear system is part of what is known as an Epi-
cyclic gear train (one or more outer gears rotating around a
central gear).
The system allows for a reduction in speed whilst increasing
the torque (underdrive) or an increase in speed whilst reduc-
ing the torque (overdrive).
Because of its capability it can be used in applications such as
vehicle automatic gear system, aircraft propeller drive shaft
and even in clocks!

The Planetary gear system works by holding any one of the
gears from rotating (reaction gear) while another gear does the
driving (input gear). The remaining gear becomes the driven
gear (output gear).

• Overdrive (vehicle automatic gear box)
• Underdrive (propellers)
• Reverse drive (reverse the output direction to the input
direction)

Large and powerful engines generate very high torque at high

as the aircraft becomes larger and the engines become more
powerful; the torque forces are much too high, even with the

Propeller designers try to achieve maximum performance
while meeting limits on diameter, weight, strength, and noise.
High efficiency comes from running the blade tip speed close

Modern propeller designs have swept back tips that act in the
same manner as a swept back wing.
Sweeping the blade tip back improves the efficiency by delay-
ing the production of shockwaves. This allows the propeller to
be rotated much faster without the tips exceeding the speed of

PROPELLER ICE INTRODUCTION
Moist air and low temperatures can cause ice to form on the
PROTECTION propeller blades. This ice will change the aerofoil shape, lead-
ing to turbulence, loss of efficiency and in extreme cases the
SYSTEMS propeller blades will stall and stop producing thrust.
Ice may also build up on the leading edges of the engine air
intake and oil cooler fairings. This could eventually cause the
engine to be starved of air and flame out. To prevent this, many
propellers are fitted with ice protection systems.
Propeller ice elimination systems are used to prevent or re-
move ice formation on propeller blades during flight. If ice is
allowed to remain on the blades the efficiency of the aerofoil is
reduced, the propeller becomes heavier, and develops an out
of balance condition. These conditions can generate vibrations
and cause damage to the engine and airframe.
DE-ICING AND ANTI-ICING SYSTEMS
An anti-icing system:
• Operates continuously to prevent ice from forming.
• Usually, anti-icing system uses the anti-icing fluid to
prevent the accumulation of the ice on the leading edge
of the propeller blade. For engine intake the electrical-
ly anti-icing can be used or a supply of heated air can
be taken from the engine and circulated in the areas
where ice build-up must be prevented.

bonded (glued) together. The process is called Lamination.

PROPELLER SAFETY
INTRODUCTION
A propeller driven aircraft with piston engines is still danger-
ous when parked in the hangar. The ignition system is always
live, and if the engine is rotated during servicing the spark
plugs will operate. If any fuel/air mixture is present they may
fire the engine.
To prevent the engine from starting; a cockpit operated safety
switch (called an ignition master switch) is connected to the
ignition circuit.
The switch will isolate the ignition circuit. This means that if Fig 06. 33 - Ignition Master Switch
the engine is turned, no spark will be produced. Operate the
switch before beginning any servicing and use signs to warn
other personnel not to operate the switch.

MOVING PROPELLER DRIVEN AIRCRAFT
When moving a propeller driven aircraft, you must always use
the correct equipment. All RAFO aircraft are provided with
Towing or Steering Arm, which may be used to manoeuvre the
aircraft on the ground.
The aircraft must never be pushed or pulled using the propel-
ler as this will cause great stress at the blade roots, especially if
the aircraft is stopped by an obstruction. This stress may lead
to eventual disastrous blade failure in flight. Therefore, never
push or pull the aircraft using the propeller.

VEHICLES AND PROPELLERS
If approaching a running aircraft in a vehicle, keep away from
the area of the propellers.
Do not stop the vehicle in front of the propellers; as people in a
hurry to board the aircraft may run through the propeller arc.
Do not leave the vehicle behind the wings, because the aircraft
may be fitted with thrust reversing propellers and use them for
manoeuvring.
Always stop the vehicle well clear of the aircraft, in a position
where it can be seen by the aircrew and driven away quickly
in an emergency.
